title: Matinee program mix
brief:
Write a programming recommendation for an independent cinema choosing six Sunday matinees. Fictional history covers two screenings per format, with totals for paid admissions, ticket revenue, concessions contribution after ingredient costs, and direct event costs. Classic comedy: 134, $1,206, $315, $700. Animated double bill: 172, $1,376, $410, $960. Local documentary: 108, $1,080, $190, $650. Silent film with live piano: 156, $2,028, $290, $1,680. Capacity is 100 per screening. Use at least three formats, include one documentary, and stay within $3,000 in direct costs. Use historical averages to build and compare feasible calendars, stress-test a 15% drop in admissions, and explain your choice to the owner.

Aim for 1,200 to 1,800 words. Return the complete original work directly in your answer. Do not sign or identify yourself. Do not use tools.

57bc5aa1753946ea.text:
I recommend booking **four classic comedies, one animated double bill, and one local documentary**. Open with a comedy, give animation the second Sunday, and put the documentary on the fourth. At historical averages, this calendar draws 408 paid admissions and earns **$2,365 after direct event costs**. It costs $2,205 to stage, leaving $795 of the owner’s $3,000 budget uncommitted. If attendance across the series falls 15%, it still earns an estimated **$1,679.50**, the highest contribution any calendar meeting the requirements can deliver in that scenario.

The closest decision is how many Sundays to give animation. An animation-led series is the better choice if the owner’s main objective is to bring the most people through the doors. It projects 57 more admissions than the recommended series. For this booking decision, I would give financial resilience more weight. Those 57 additional admissions yield just $7.50 more contribution across six Sundays at historical turnout, while requiring $390 more in direct spending.

### What each Sunday earns

The supplied figures are totals for two screenings of each format, so each entry below is half the corresponding historical total. “Event contribution” means ticket revenue plus concessions contribution after ingredient costs, less direct event costs. It measures what the matinee leaves to cover the cinema’s overhead. Ingredient costs have already been deducted from concessions and are counted only once.

| Format | Paid admissions | Ticket revenue | Concessions contribution | Direct cost | Event contribution |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Classic comedy | 67 | $603 | $157.50 | $350 | $410.50 |
| Animated double bill | 86 | $688 | $205 | $480 | $413 |
| Local documentary | 54 | $540 | $95 | $325 | $310 |
| Silent film with live piano | 78 | $1,014 | $145 | $840 | $319 |

Animation has the strongest recorded turnout, averaging 86 of the available 100 seats. It also generates the most concessions contribution per screening. The reason comedy can compete at just 67 admissions is visible in two figures. Animation brings in an extra $132.50 from tickets and concessions combined, and costs an extra $130 to present. Nearly all the additional income is committed before the screening begins.

The documentary makes a useful contribution in its own right. Its historical audience fills just over half the room, yet the screening earns $310 on the smallest direct outlay of the four formats. Live piano makes a different proposition. At an average realized ticket price of $13, it produces the highest box office of the group. Its $840 direct cost, however, leaves only $319 after the event, just $9 more than the documentary earns for a $325 commitment. A piano screening would buy the program a distinctive live event, but its premium ticket price alone is a weak financial reason to book it.

### Four feasible calendars

Each option below fills six Sundays, includes the documentary, uses at least three formats, and fits the direct-cost ceiling. All projected screening audiences are within the 100-seat limit. The admissions column counts visits across the series, so a patron attending twice contributes two admissions.

| Six-Sunday mix | Paid admissions | Direct costs | Event contribution | Contribution with 15% fewer admissions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 comedies, 1 animation, 1 documentary | 408 | $2,205 | $2,365.00 | $1,679.50 |
| 3 comedies, 2 animations, 1 documentary | 427 | $2,335 | $2,367.50 | $1,662.13 |
| 1 comedy, 4 animations, 1 documentary | 465 | $2,595 | $2,372.50 | $1,627.38 |
| 3 comedies, 1 animation, 1 documentary, 1 live piano | 419 | $2,695 | $2,273.50 | $1,528.23 |

The animation-led option earns the highest contribution possible at historical averages. With one documentary required, animation is the highest earner for each remaining slot, and comedy is the most profitable third format. Four animated double bills therefore make sense for an owner who values admissions growth and is comfortable committing $2,595. The two-animation calendar offers a smaller step in that direction. Against the recommendation, it buys 19 additional projected visits for $130 more in direct costs, with a $2.50 improvement in expected contribution.

The four-format calendar puts a price on variety. Replacing one recommended comedy with live piano adds 11 projected admissions and brings a live performance to the series. It also commits another $490 and reduces expected contribution by $91.50. An owner planning a special occasion might willingly make that exchange. For six regular Sunday bookings, the documentary and animated double bill already give audiences two distinct reasons to visit alongside comedy, at a lower cost.

### How the recommendation holds up

For the stress test, I reduced attendance at every screening by 15%, kept each format’s average ticket revenue and concessions contribution per admission constant, and held direct event costs fixed. This assumes the cinema has committed to presenting the events even if fewer people come. It also preserves differences in spending between formats. A lost admission at the $13 silent film has a different box-office effect from a lost admission at the $8 animated double bill.

For the recommended series, baseline ticket revenue is $3,640 and concessions contribute $930. A 15% attendance decline takes those figures to $3,094 and $790.50. After the same $2,205 in direct costs, the cinema keeps $1,679.50. Expected attendance falls from 408 to about 347 visits. I applied the percentage before rounding attendance, so the financial estimate reflects the full 15% change.

The stressed contribution per screening is about $296.43 for comedy, $279.05 for animation, $214.75 for documentary, and $145.15 for live piano. That ordering explains why the recommended mix leads across all feasible calendars. Once the documentary is booked, animation is the strongest third format to pair with comedy, and each remaining Sunday earns the most from another comedy. The shift in ranking starts well before the full stress case. Animation’s ordinary $2.50 lead disappears when a common attendance decline exceeds about 1.9%, because animation has $132.50 more attendance-dependent income per screening. With only two historical screenings behind each average, I would give little weight to a lead that narrow.

### Putting the six Sundays on sale

| Sunday | Booking | Programming purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Classic comedy | Open with a stand-alone title that introduces the comedy selection. |
| 2 | Animated double bill | Give the double feature its own early date and advertise the full running time. |
| 3 | Classic comedy | Choose a different comic style or era from the opener. |
| 4 | Local documentary | Give the local subject a featured Sunday and lead the listing with its connection to the community. |
| 5 | Classic comedy | Return to comedy with a title that works independently of the earlier screenings. |
| 6 | Classic comedy | Close with the title the cinema considers the strongest draw of its comedy selection. |

The sequence spaces the two specialist formats across the first four weeks. The main programming risk is the run of four comedies, particularly the consecutive dates at the end. The history establishes an average for two comedy screenings. It cannot establish whether four titles in six weeks will sustain the same audience. I would select the final pair together and give each a distinct selling point in the listings so regular patrons can see a reason to attend both. The projections assume each comedy performs at its format average and give no financial credit for title selection, publicity, or repeat visits beyond that average.

For the owner, the decision comes down to what the additional booking dollars purchase. A second animated Sunday is defensible if 19 more projected visits matter enough to justify another $130 commitment. The historical figures give little reason to spend that money for earnings alone. Four comedies, the animated double bill, and the local documentary preserve nearly all the historical upside, give the community film a featured date, and leave the cinema with the strongest contribution if turnout softens.

7b225989baaf9fe4.text:
# Sunday matinee programming recommendation

Book **four classic comedies, one animated double bill, and one local documentary**. The six Sundays are projected to draw **408 paid admissions** and contribute **$2,365** after direct event costs. The calendar costs **$2,205** to put on, leaving **$795** of the $3,000 budget available. If admissions fall 15% across the series, the projected contribution is **$1,679.50**, the highest of any calendar that meets the programming requirements.

The strongest calendar for attendance puts four animated double bills on the schedule. It would draw 57 more paid admissions at the historical averages, which is a meaningful difference if the owner wants to bring as many people through the doors as possible. Its projected contribution advantage is only **$7.50**. For this run, I would prioritize the calendar that delivers nearly the same contribution at the historical averages, commits less cash, and earns more in the requested downside scenario.

## What the historical screenings tell us

Each format has two screenings in the fictional history. Dividing each total by two gives the per-screening estimates below. Contribution is ticket revenue plus concessions contribution after ingredient costs, less direct event costs. It measures what the series contributes toward the cinema’s other expenses and overall result.

| Format | Paid admissions | Ticket revenue | Concessions contribution | Direct cost | Net contribution |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| Classic comedy | 67 | $603 | $157.50 | $350 | $410.50 |
| Animated double bill | 86 | $688 | $205 | $480 | $413.00 |
| Local documentary | 54 | $540 | $95 | $325 | $310.00 |
| Silent film with live piano | 78 | $1,014 | $145 | $840 | $319.00 |

With 100 seats per screening, the admissions column also gives each format’s average occupancy percentage. The animated double bill fills the most seats and generates the most concessions contribution. It also costs $130 more to stage than a comedy. At the historical averages, its additional ticket and concessions contribution comes to $132.50, leaving just $2.50 of additional net contribution per booking.

The silent film with live piano has the highest ticket revenue, at an implied $13 per paid admission. It also has the highest direct cost, at $840 per Sunday. It can fit within the budget, and it offers a distinct live event, but the historical numbers put its contribution below both the comedy and the double bill. The documentary has the lowest average attendance and the lowest direct cost. One booking fulfills the local documentary requirement and makes room for a local program within a six-week run.

## Feasible calendars

Each calendar below has six screenings, includes a documentary, uses at least three formats, and stays within the direct-cost cap. Financial results for the stress test are rounded to cents after calculating the series totals.

| Six-Sunday mix | Paid admissions | Direct cost | Net contribution at historical averages | Net contribution with 15% fewer admissions |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| **4 comedies, 1 animated double bill, 1 documentary** | **408** | **$2,205** | **$2,365.00** | **$1,679.50** |
| 3 comedies, 2 animated double bills, 1 documentary | 427 | $2,335 | $2,367.50 | $1,662.13 |
| 2 comedies, 3 animated double bills, 1 documentary | 446 | $2,465 | $2,370.00 | $1,644.75 |
| 1 comedy, 4 animated double bills, 1 documentary | 465 | $2,595 | $2,372.50 | $1,627.38 |
| 3 comedies, 1 animated double bill, 1 documentary, 1 silent film with live piano | 419 | $2,695 | $2,273.50 | $1,528.23 |

The first four rows show the decision in one-screening increments. For every comedy replaced by an animated double bill, the cinema projects **19 more paid admissions**, spends **$130 more**, and gains **$2.50** in contribution at the historical averages. Under the attendance stress test, each of those swaps reduces contribution by **$17.38** when rounded to cents. The middle calendars are viable if the owner wants a larger audience and still wants comedy to account for at least a third of the series.

At historical averages, four double bills deliver the highest projected contribution. Animation leads on per-screening contribution, and after reserving one Sunday for the documentary, comedy is the strongest remaining format to satisfy the three-format requirement. The 15% drop changes the ranking. Comedy leads on stressed contribution per screening, and the double bill remains the strongest choice for the third format alongside comedy and the required documentary. That makes four comedies the best-performing mix in the downside case.

The four-format calendar shows what it would cost to include the live piano event. Replacing a comedy with it buys 11 more projected paid admissions and adds $490 in direct costs. Series contribution falls by $91.50 at the historical averages and by $151.28 in the stress test, using the unrounded estimates for the comparison. The live performance could warrant that trade if presenting it is a programming priority. The stated requirements can be met with a higher projected contribution and a lower commitment.

## How the attendance stress test works

The test assumes 15% fewer paid admissions at every screening, with ticket revenue and concessions contribution falling in the same proportion. This holds the historical average ticket revenue and concessions contribution per admission steady. Direct event costs stay fixed at the booking estimates. Fractional admissions in the calculation represent projections.

For the recommended mix, the historical averages yield **$3,640 in ticket revenue** and **$930 in concessions contribution**. A 15% decline brings those figures to **$3,094** and **$790.50**, respectively. Subtracting the same $2,205 in direct costs leaves **$1,679.50**. Projected attendance falls from 408 to about 347 across 600 available seats, or from **68% to about 58% occupancy**.

The most animation-heavy calendar starts with a higher projected occupancy of **77.5%**, so it has a clear advantage on audience volume. It also has more revenue and concessions contribution tied to turnout and a higher fixed cost. Under the same proportional assumptions, a uniform admissions decline of about **1.9%** would erase its $7.50 contribution lead over the recommended calendar. With just two historical screenings per format, a difference that small is well within the uncertainty around turnout. The 15% scenario is a sensitivity test. Actual results will depend on the titles booked, the audiences they draw, and what those audiences spend.

## Proposed Sunday lineup

| Sunday | Format | Programming purpose |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Classic comedy | Open with a recognizable title that can introduce the series. |
| 2 | Animated double bill | Give families an early date and a distinct program to plan around. |
| 3 | Classic comedy | Choose a different era or style from the opener. |
| 4 | Local documentary | Give the local film its own Sunday and a clear focus in the series promotion. |
| 5 | Classic comedy | Use a title that broadens the range of the comedy selections. |
| 6 | Classic comedy | Close with a title that has broad audience appeal. |

The sequence is an editorial choice. The projections use the same format averages regardless of which Sunday a screening occupies. Four distinct comedy titles give returning patrons a reason to come back, while placing the double bill and documentary in the first four weeks gives both formats an early place in the series.

I would approve the **$2,205 calendar** and keep the **$795** in budget headroom uncommitted. The cinema gets six Sundays with three formats, a dedicated local documentary screening, and almost all the projected contribution of the highest-attendance option. The extra animated bookings are worth considering if the owner puts a premium on the additional 57 projected admissions. On the stated budget and downside test, four comedies give the series the stronger financial footing.

f760adeb53ce3ab8.text:
# Sunday Matinee Programming Recommendation

## Recommendation

Program **three classic comedies, two animated double bills and one local documentary**. On historical averages this calendar contributes about **$2,368** across the six Sundays on **$2,335** of direct costs, which leaves $665 of the $3,000 budget unspent. If admissions fall 15% across the board, it still contributes about **$1,662**.

No feasible calendar does meaningfully better. The top four options sit within $8 of each other in the base case, so the choice comes down to resilience and variety rather than headline return.

## What each format earns per screening

Dividing each format's two-screening totals by two gives a per-screening average. Contribution here means ticket revenue plus concessions contribution, minus direct event costs.

| Format | Admissions | Tickets | Concessions | Direct cost | Contribution | Return per $1 of cost |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Classic comedy | 67 | $603.00 | $157.50 | $350 | **$410.50** | $1.17 |
| Animated double bill | 86 | $688.00 | $205.00 | $480 | **$413.00** | $0.86 |
| Local documentary | 54 | $540.00 | $95.00 | $325 | **$310.00** | $0.95 |
| Silent film with live piano | 78 | $1,014.00 | $145.00 | $840 | **$319.00** | $0.38 |

Three things stand out:

- **Comedy and animation are effectively tied.** They are $2.50 apart per screening, far less than the noise in a two-screening sample. Comedy gets there on $130 less cost.
- **The silent film takes the most money and keeps the least of it.** It has the highest ticket price ($13 average) and the highest gross, but the $840 cost absorbs most of that. It contributes about $90 less than a comedy while putting more than twice the money at risk.
- **The documentary is the weakest draw but cheap to run.** One documentary is required, and at $310 it earns nearly as much as the silent film.

No format averaged above the 100-seat capacity, so every average is usable as it stands. Capacity does limit upside: the animated bill averages 86, leaving only 14 seats of headroom on a good day, against 33 for comedy.

## Which calendars are feasible

The rules are six screenings, at least three formats, at least one documentary and no more than $3,000 in direct costs. They have one consequence that is not obvious at first glance: **two silent screenings can never fit.** Two silents cost $1,680. The cheapest legal way to fill the other four slots (one documentary and three comedies) costs $1,375, for a total of $3,055. Every other three-format combination with two silents also exceeds the budget. So the real choice is between calendars with one silent film and calendars with none.

## Comparing the calendars

The stress case assumes admissions fall 15% for every screening, ticket revenue and concessions fall in proportion, and direct costs stay fixed.

| Calendar | Comedy | Animated | Doc | Silent | Direct cost | Base contribution | Stressed contribution |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 1 | 4 | 1 | 0 | $2,595 | $2,372.50 | $1,627.38 |
| B | 2 | 3 | 1 | 0 | $2,465 | $2,370.00 | $1,644.75 |
| **C (recommended)** | **3** | **2** | **1** | **0** | **$2,335** | **$2,367.50** | **$1,662.13** |
| D | 4 | 1 | 1 | 0 | $2,205 | $2,365.00 | $1,679.50 |
| E | 2 | 2 | 2 | 0 | $2,310 | $2,267.00 | $1,580.45 |
| F | 3 | 1 | 1 | 1 | $2,695 | $2,273.50 | $1,528.23 |
| G | 2 | 2 | 1 | 1 | $2,825 | $2,276.00 | $1,510.85 |

Calendars A to D differ by $7.50 in the base case, which is a tie. The stress test separates them: each animated bill swapped for a comedy adds about $17 of protection, because comedy carries less fixed cost. Calendars with a second documentary or a silent film give up roughly $90 to $100 in the base case and more under stress.

## How each format handles a bad day

Because costs are fixed, a 15% fall in attendance reduces contribution by more than 15%.

| Format | Base contribution | After a 15% drop | Admissions needed to break even | Fall from average it can absorb |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Classic comedy | $410.50 | $296.43 | about 31 | about 54% |
| Animated double bill | $413.00 | $279.05 | about 47 | about 45% |
| Local documentary | $310.00 | $214.75 | about 28 | about 48% |
| Silent film with live piano | $319.00 | $145.15 | about 57 | about 27% |

The silent film loses more than half its contribution in the stress case and starts losing money once attendance falls about a quarter below its average. The other three formats can lose close to half their audience before a screening loses money.

For the recommended calendar, the stress case looks like this:

| | Base | 15% drop |
|---|---|---|
| Paid admissions | 427 | about 363 |
| Ticket revenue | $3,725.00 | $3,166.25 |
| Concessions contribution | $977.50 | $830.88 |
| Direct costs | $2,335.00 | $2,335.00 |
| **Contribution** | **$2,367.50** | **$1,662.13** |

A 15% fall in attendance cuts contribution by about 30%, but the series stays comfortably positive.

## Why Calendar C and not the others

**Why not D, which is slightly stronger under stress?** D leads C by $17 in the stress case and trails it by $2.50 in the base case. Neither gap is large enough to act on, since each format's average rests on two screenings. D asks the same comedy audience to turn out four Sundays out of six, and the averages cannot tell us whether the fourth comedy draws 67 people or 45. C spreads the series across two strong formats that draw different audiences, so one misjudged format does less damage. If you would rather keep the extra $130 in reserve and are confident in the comedy audience, D is a reasonable alternative.

**Why not A or B, which top the base case?** Their $2.50 to $5 lead is not meaningful, and they cost $130 to $260 more and hold up worse under stress. The animated bill is also nearest to capacity, so it has the least room to beat its average.

**Why no silent film?** It is the costliest slot and the most fragile one. Swapping one comedy for the silent film (Calendar G) costs about $92 in expected contribution and about $151 in the stress case, and it raises direct costs by $490. That may still be worth doing for reasons these numbers do not capture, such as press attention, the higher ticket price, or goodwill with patrons and musicians. If you want it, G is the version to run, treating the roughly $92 as the cost of a prestige event rather than expecting it to pay its way.

**Why only one documentary?** A second one (Calendar E) costs about $100 in contribution against C. One screening meets the requirement and keeps the local-filmmaker relationship alive.

## Caveats

- **The sample is thin.** Two screenings per format cannot distinguish a $2.50 difference, and barely support a $90 one. Treat the rankings among comedy and animation as a tie, and the gap to the silent film as likely but unproven.
- **Repetition is untested.** The history shows two screenings per format, and this plan runs comedy three times. Alternating formats across the six Sundays, rather than running comedies back to back, should limit audience fatigue.
- **The unspent budget is a cushion.** The plan leaves $665 unspent, and I would keep it as a buffer rather than upgrade a slot.
- **The series will improve the data.** Recording admissions, ticket revenue, concessions and costs for each Sunday will bring comedy to five data points and animation to four, which gives the next programming decision much firmer ground.
